items.title: ‘Totally Demonic’: Jonathan Cahn Reveals What Really Happened With the Viral Duct-Taped Man on Plane
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Whoa.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Celebrated author and Messianic rabbi Jonathan Cahn is making headlines after revealing that he was the unnamed passenger who drew the ire of an allegedly irate man who was so out of control he needed to be duct taped to an airplane seat.

Cahn shared his account of the disturbing incident aboard American Airlines Flight 618, proclaiming that the widely circulated images of a passenger being duct-taped — and media accounts of what unfolded — did not tell the full story.

He told CBN News he was returning home after a number of interviews promoting his new book, “The Altar of Pergamon,” when his assigned seat was unexpectedly changed shortly before the flight. Little did he know that his new placement on the plane would yield an experience he’d never forget.

Cahn ended up sitting beside a man who he said initially appeared friendly. In fact, the two talked for roughly two hours, with the passenger asking about his books and discussing his own family — but then the situation shifted after Cahn prayed about whether God wanted him to share his faith with the man.

“I said, ‘Give me an opening to share salvation with him, and share love with him,’” he said.

According to Cahn, the conversation turned toward faith, and he shared his testimony of once being an atheist and eventually coming to believe in God. Then, he said, the man’s behavior abruptly changed.

“At that moment, I’ve never seen anything like this,” he said. “His face changes. His voice changes.”

Cahn described the transformation as dramatic and spiritual, saying, “It was like someone getting taken over.”

He said the passenger began cursing Jesus and God, making vulgar statements and disturbing other people aboard the aircraft. Cahn said the man later became friendly again before allegedly putting his hands around Cahn’s neck and lightly striking him.

One of the most unusual moments involved Cahn’s laptop. At one point, a black line appeared on his screen. He said the passenger then reached over and tapped the computer, forcing the black area to spread across the entire screen.

Cahn said the computer was particularly important because it contained his writings and other projects.

Then, the author felt God tell him to protect his computer because the devil would use the man to destroy it. Listening to this warning, he attempted to leave his seat with the laptop and alleged that this is when the passenger lunged for it.

“We are wrestling on the plane,” Cahn said, noting that the computer became the focal point of the chaos. “I mean, we are literally wrestling.”

Cahn said the pilot contacted the ground for an emergency landing as the confrontation continued. Eventually, two passengers, including a retired police officer, intervened. Flight attendants provided duct tape to restrain the man, and the plane landed in Baltimore, where authorities took the man into custody.

The irony of the entire incident is that Cohn’s latest book “The Altar of Pergamon” — which came out just before this incident — deals with themes surrounding the devil and spiritual warfare. He believes some of what unfolded on the flight is rooted in that spiritual battle.

“The warfare is real, the enemy is real, and God is real,” he said.

Despite what happened, Cahn said he has no desire to condemn the passenger. Instead, he said he prays for him, and he even delivered a message to him.

“God loves you,” he said. “God’s arms are open. He loves you and He’ll receive you and wash that all away and give you a new beginning.”

Watch the full interview for more on this shocking story.

items.title: Southern Miss Football Coach Makes Bold Faith Declaration Ahead of Big Win
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: Inspiring.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Football season is just now getting underway, but Southern Miss head coach Blake Anderson drew a lot of attention before his players ever hit the gridiron Saturday.

Ahead of kickoff, Anderson wore a black long-sleeve shirt with the words “Christ Is King” emblazoned in yellow letters across the chest as he and the University of Southern Mississippi team performed took part in the “Eagle Walk” to the stadium.

The team went on to win an impressive 49-3 victory against Alcorn State University.

“I’ve had a bunch of people comment, and I’m pleased that it was noticed,” Anderson said during his weekly press conference. “I mean, the whole point of wearing it was for Christ to be glorified and it to be noticed.”

“I’m super grateful for my bosses that allowed me to be religious [and] use my platform to share my faith,” he continued. “[That is] not probably an easy decision for an AD and a president. But, you know, those are my views. That’s just me trying to use my platform.”

Anderson went on to say he is “saved by grace” and credited God with his success as a coach.

While bold public stances like his often garner criticism, the head football coach said he is thankful the responses online have been overwhelmingly positive.

“You never know what kind of response you’re going to get,” he admitted. “It’s been 99% positive and a few negative, which is what I expected. I wasn’t completely aware of just where it would go.”

He added, “In my opinion, if it makes one person think, then it was worth it.”

Anderson has been vocal about his faith for several years, even through incredible tragedies.

His wife, Wendy, died of breast cancer in 2019, followed soon after by the passing of his father. Anderson’s son, Cason, took his life in 2022, and the coach’s brother, Bryan, died in 2024, following a lengthy battle with aggressive colon cancer.

One of Anderson’s close friends, Larry Fedora, said he “wouldn’t have been able to survive if he didn’t have such a strong faith.”

In 2020, when he was the head coach of Utah State, Anderson told local reporters, “I’m a Christian before I’m anything else. I love the Lord and I feel like God put me in coaching.”

And in an interview five years later with Football Scoop, he said, “My faith comes from Christ, not from me. I’m not tough enough, I’m not big enough to do this on my own.”

items.title: Tori Kelly Performed Her Album ‘God Must Really Love Me’ on NPR’s Tiny Desk
items.author: RELEVANT Staff
items.summary: NPR’s Tiny Desk is the least forgiving stage in music. No effects, no lighting, no crowd to disappear into — just a musician standing a few feet from a room of NPR employees, in front of a bookshelf. Tori Kelly played it this week, performing seven songs — six of them off her latest album,&#82
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

NPR’s Tiny Desk is the least forgiving stage in music. No effects, no lighting, no crowd to disappear into — just a musician standing a few feet from a room of NPR employees, in front of a bookshelf.

Tori Kelly played it this week, performing seven songs — six of them off her latest album, God Must Really Love Me — with an all-woman band.

The set included “Hurts So Good,” “Without You,” “Fly,” “Bird,” “Control” and “Tokyo,” plus a cover of Stevie Wonder’s “Don’t You Worry ‘Bout a Thing.” She played guitar on some of it and, at one point, a toy glockenspiel.

The cover came with an explanation: “Have y’all heard of the movie ‘Sing’?” she asked the room. “So do you know Meena the elephant? That’s me.”

She voiced Meena in the animated film and sang that song in it. “It was so much fun being Meena that I wanted to do her song from the movie,” she said. “It’s by the legendary Stevie Wonder.”

God Must Really Love Me came out in June, her sixth album. It isn’t her first record in this territory — Hiding Place, in 2018, was a full gospel album made with Kirk Franklin, and it won her a Grammy.

In introducing “Bird,” she opened up.

“This song in particular,” she said. “I just got really vulnerable one day, and I was just hit with a wave of anxiety. And this world is crazy, y’all. This world is really, really crazy. And so I just put all those feelings into this song.”

items.title: Dispelling the Darkness of September 11
items.author: Fr. Steve Grunow
items.summary:
Fr. Steve Grunow

God in Christ went into the suffering, the death. It was as if a million World Trade Centers passed through him, and he took it all into himself.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Fr. Steve Grunow

Suddenly summoned to witness something great and horrendous, we keep fighting not to reduce it to our own smallness.

These are the words of the writer, the late John Updike, as he described September 11, 2001. It was an event that yielded the terrible destruction of not only one of the most famous monuments of our civilization but of so many lives, and it left a wound on the national psyche that still stings us today.

Updike watched the catastrophe unfold from an apartment in Brooklyn Heights. While many of us witnessed the event through the screens of our TVs, Updike saw it from the vantage point of his apartment’s window. Then moving to the roof of his building, he saw the fire, “the smoke speckled with the bits of paper curled into the cloudless sky.” And finally, in one of the longest instants of time many of us have ever experienced, those mammoth towers dropped, falling straight down “like an elevator with a tinkling shiver and groan of concussion distinct across a mile of air.”

Updike wrote, “We knew that we had just witnessed thousands of deaths; and we clung to each other as if we ourselves were falling.”

We caught ourselves in mid-flight, it seems. Reckoning with the loss, grief gave way to anger and then more grief. Cries for justice. The war-machine of the nation stirred to life, and the map of the world became so much bigger than we had previously assumed. Our tongues tripped over foreign names and far off places. We witnessed and celebrated heroes—searched for, then dreamed of, survivors. We buried the dead. We cared for widows and orphans. We prayed through all our doubts. We surrendered our illusions. We cleared the wreckage. We wondered what to do next.

And in all of this, we were fighting not to reduce what we had seen, what we had witnessed, to our own smallness.

Since then, there have been many more disappointments. It has been as if the light that had been shining on our national psyche has gone out. There has been a power failure of sorts that has sapped our supply of cultural energy.

Everything seems smaller. The world seems so much larger. We feel so much more vulnerable. If those towers could fall so fast, if so few could do such great harm, if so many could be lost in an instant, what about me? What about all of us?

Though we may no longer be falling, we still cling to one another.

Christian faith believes that evil manifests itself in two mysteries: the absence of the good, what St. Augustine called the “privatio bonum,” which is not so much anything at all, but an emptiness, a lack—kind of like the darkness we experience in the absence of light. But evil is also known to us as a presence, a malevolence, an entity that has hated us from before any of us were made. Both are before us as temptation and tempter. The temptation is to fall into the illusion that there is something to be gained in evil deeds, that we can take the nothing of evil and makes it into something and in doing so gain some kind of benefit when there is no reward at all. The tempter seeks to entice us with evil and then insinuates into our minds a dreadful fear that we can justify our hate by insisting that God demands victims.

We shudder at these beliefs and spend perhaps too little time with them, for the implications of both forms of evil frighten us so.

But this is not, after all, all that we believe.

We believe that God, in his greatness, becomes small like us, and concentrated within that smallness is a love that knows no bounds. God in Christ came into the world with the express purpose of going into the emptiness of evil and facing down the evil one, and in doing so, he assured us that when all is said and done, it is he—not evil or the evil one—who will have the last word.

To accomplish this, God in Christ went into it all—the suffering, the death. It was as if a million World Trade Centers passed through him, and he took it all into himself. Passing through the darkness, he came back to us, and thereby showed that nothing, not even suffering and death, can separate us from him. Despite how things appear, despite how they feel, he is active, working, transforming, sanctifying, redeeming—even in the heart of our worst darkness. We call this the Paschal Mystery. And it happens to us all the time—on September 11, 2001, and every day—until all things are brought to their fulfillment in him.

It is this mystery of God become small in Christ, of love penetrating suffering and death, that reveals to us that there is not just a gaping hole in the midst of that empty space we call Ground Zero, and in all the Ground Zeros that have beset us from even before the foundations of the world were laid.

Today, we remember those events—the fire, the smoke speckled with bits of paper curled into the cloudless sky, those towers falling straight down like an elevator, the reverberations of the crashing planes that still makes us all unsteady.

But that is not all we remember.

We remember the dead—not as lost, but as living in him. We hope in our faith that in all those moments when a great darkness descends, God in Christ is with us; he has us all in his view. It was for their sake and all our sakes that he gave himself to us in his Paschal Mystery. And in that moment of terror when this world gives way to darkness, our hope is that he is there as the Divine Light that dispels the darkness and guides us to that holiest of places, which is his kingdom yet to come.

Eternal rest grant unto them O Lord, and let perpetual light shine upon them.

This piece was originally published on September 11, 2017, on Evangelization & Culture Online.

items.title: The Virtue of Stability in the Vocation of the Writer
items.author: Peter Keepman
items.summary:
Peter Keepman

A hidden gem of O’Connor’s corpus is her thought on the vocation of the fiction writer, a vocation animated by an almost Benedictine spirit of stability.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Peter Keepman

This year marks the sixty-second anniversary of Flannery O’Connor’s death. The great “hillbilly Thomist” and writer is most famous for her gothic short stories and novels such as “Good Country People,” A Good Man Is Hard to Find, and Wiseblood. A hidden gem of O’Connor’s corpus, however, is her own thought on the vocation of the fiction writer, a vocation animated by an almost Benedictine spirit of stability. In a post-modern milieu where genius is associated with madness and those who pursue writing, art, music, or poetry are characterized by eccentricity, reading O’Connor’s thoughts in conversation with The Rule of St. Benedict, reveal a different model for the Catholic creative and intellectual.

The Vocation of the Fiction Writer

There is no shortage of pop culture examples associating genius with madness, particularly in cinema. Movies in the last forty years such as A Beautiful Mind, Pollock, Camille, Maestro, and Last Call all depict real-life examples of creatives who suffered mental health issues, had exacting personalities, or had habits and practices that were eccentric. Moreover, that association—between genius and madness—has roots in the Classical tradition, as seen in works such as Plato’s Phaedrus where he speaks of “divine madness” in relation to beauty. Implicitly or explicitly, our culture seems to take that correlation and think of it as causation; to be a good intellectual and creative, one must have a touch of madness or eccentricity. The popular phrase misattributed to Hemingway, “Write drunk, edit sober,” reflects this view.

O’Connor’s vision of the creative occupations, specifically fiction writing, is different. For O’Connor, fiction writing is a vocation and thinks that one hears the call to become a fiction writer by recognizing the gifts within him or herself. As she says in her essay “The Nature and Aim of Fiction,” “There is no excuse for anyone to write fiction for public consumption unless he has been called to do so by the presence of a gift. It is the nature of fiction not to be good for much unless it is good in itself.” Having recognized these gifts, the vocation of fiction writing is one ordered towards elucidating truth “both in matter and in mode . . . in an imaginative sense.” The fiction writer’s vocation is to mediate truth through story, a distinct task from elucidating truth as such, something proper to the role of the philosopher or theologian. 

Aiming at truth “in an imaginative sense” means that the writer takes an incarnational view of all reality, dealing neither in pure spirit nor pure matter. Rather, echoing Aristotle and Aquinas, O’Connor believes the artist knows firstly through his senses and recognizes that the created things in this world reflect in some way the goodness of the Creator. As O’Connor says in her essay “Novelist and Believer,” “The artist penetrates the concrete world in order to find at its depths the image of its source, the image of ultimate reality.” As anyone who has read O’Connor’s short stories knows, however, this incarnational view does not blind the writer to human frailty, evil, or any other privation of the good. Rather, as O’Connor explains, it “sharpens it, for only when the natural world is seen as good, does evil become intelligible as a destructive force and a necessary result of our freedom.” O’Connor’s openness to recognizing humanity’s pitfalls and the presence of evil in her own writing led many to accuse O’Connor of being nihilistic. However, O’Connor recognized that in the midst of evil, grace is always at play. The vocation of the fiction writer is one directed toward recognizing the interplay between nature and grace and the latter’s operation amidst human brokenness.

Implicit in O’Connor’s overall vision of the fiction writer’s vocation is a disposition of stability. Without it, the writer risks losing his or her keen powers of observation that allow for the incarnational view of all reality and the recognition of the interplay of nature and grace. Seeing reality clearly requires taking a long view of things, and a writer living a frenetic life is not disposed to taking that view. Those wanting a deeper understanding of the kind of stability O’Connor implies can find it in a much older source: The Rule of St. Benedict by St. Benedict of Nursia. 

Stability in the Rule of St. Benedict

The Rule of St. Benedict was devised by St. Benedict for his monastic communities, the Benedictines, sometime after 530 AD, after he had founded the Abbey of Monte Cassino. Fundamentally, following The Rule involves giving up one’s own will to follow the will of God. The life of Benedictine monks is ordered around work and prayer, or ora et labora, and The Rule integrates those two tenets into a consistent pattern of life. Hence, The Rule prescribes that monks pray seven times a day, do spiritual readings, and perform manual labor each day.

Undergirding all of The Rule is stability. Stability is a prerequisite for discerning the monastic vocation and is one of the three vows The Rule prescribes for monks, along with fidelity to monastic life and obedience. The degree to which monks embrace stability, St. Benedict believes, is also an indication of a monk’s virtue. In the very first chapter of his Rule, St. Benedict explains that there are four kinds of monks: the cenobites, who live in a monastery guided by a rule and an abbot; the anchorites, who live as hermits in imitation of the Desert Fathers; the sarabaites, who are the “most detestable kind of monks” because of their weak character and worldliness; and lastly, the gyrovagues, the monks St. Benedict finds even worse than the sarabaites. St. Benedict describes gyrovagues as those “who spend their entire lives drifting from region to region, staying as guests for three or four days in different monasteries. Always on the move, they never settle down and are slaves to their own wills and gross appetites.” For St. Benedict, the gyrovagues are so odious because they fail to heed the basic tenet of monastic life: stability of place, the commitment to live out one’s vocation at a particular monastery for the entirety of one’s life.

Stability for St. Benedict also refers to one’s interior life, as in the constant raising of the heart and mind to God aided by a routine of prayer and work. Indeed, St. Benedict thinks it is foundational for performing good Christian works. In chapter four of The Rule, St. Benedict delineates these works at length, starting with obeying the Ten Commandments, then the corporal and spiritual works of mercy, and then moving to other admonitions, such as “Live in fear of judgment day” and “never lose hope in God’s mercy.” He concludes by saying, “The workshop where we are to toil faithfully at all these tasks is the enclosure of the monastery and stability in the community” (emphasis added).

Though O’Connor does not explicitly cite The Rule of St. Benedict in her essays on the vocation of the fiction writer, O’Connor’s own lived example as a fiction writer and her thoughts outlined above make The Rule an appropriate source to flesh out O’Connor’s understanding of a good fiction writer. O’Connor’s daily writing routine shared some aspects of the monastic life: She writes in a letter to a longtime anonymous correspondent known as “A” that she says “Prime in the morning” and “sometimes . . . Compline at night,” two of the daily monastic hours of prayer. She had a consistent routine of theological reading, explaining in another letter to A that she reads St. Thomas’s Summa theologiae for twenty minutes every night. Her writing routine was also consistent. She wrote for two hours each morning and would then spend her afternoon writing correspondence or seeing visitors. And furthermore, O’Connor was familiar with manual labor, living with her mom on their small farm, Andalusia, in Milledgeville, Georgia. 

O’Connor also criticizes her own version of St. Benedict’s gyrovagues when she assails those would‑be writers who are caught up in their own emotion. She writes in “The Nature and Aim of Fiction”:

Everywhere I go I’m asked if I think the universities stifle writers. My opinion is that they don’t stifle enough of them. There’s many a best-seller that could have been prevented by a good teacher. The idea of being a writer attracts a good many shiftless people, those who are merely burdened with poetic feelings or afflicted with sensibility” (emphasis added).

For O’Connor, as for St. Benedict, stability is not only a stability of place, but also a stability of the interior life. 

Though The Rule of St. Benedict has a particular monastic context, the lay fiction writer can nonetheless draw wisdom from those Benedictine tenets of stability, prayer, and work. By giving a fixed order to one’s life—when to eat, when to pray, when to work, when to recreate—one is not distracted by figuring out the practicals of constituting one’s day and can focus instead on sharpening one’s incarnational vision. For those aspiring to live the writing vocation O’Connor describes, St. Benedict’s Rule suggests the following five practices: 

1. Write consistently from a fixed geographic location but also a fixed place within it.

St. Benedict teaches us that in order to penetrate deeply into reality, we need to limit the number of changes we have in our experience of the outside world. Writing from a fixed location focuses the mind away from new experiences of scenery and brings it to attention on deeper human experiences. Indeed, Flannery O’Connor herself said that most of a writer’s good material came from his or her childhood, not from adult travels. 

2. Write only for a set amount of time during a set time of day.

Taking an incarnational view of reality and ordering one’s day accordingly means avoiding having intellectual work that is totalizing or all-consuming. Setting fixed start and end times for writing ensures this.

3. Have some kind of craft or physical activity that complements the writing each day.

This goes toward the work element of the Benedictine rule.

4. Set aside time to welcome friends or correspond with guests.

In the Benedictine tradition, encountering the other is an opportunity to encounter Christ. On the natural level, it also draws a person out of himself, helping him avoid being caught up in his own head.

5. And lastly and most importantly, root your day in prayer, recognizing that the reality from which you’re observing is governed by God, the author of reality itself.

Aside from the obvious good of giving thanks and praise to God, prayer is another way of drawing a person outside of himself—something important for the writer as he or she seeks to avoid the sentimentality that comes from indulging one’s ego.

Ultimately, St. Benedict’s Rule and Flannery O’Connor’s vocational vision point towards a different model for the Catholic creative and intellectual. While popular culture and even high culture suggest that a spark of madness and eccentricity is necessary in order to be a genius, O’Connor advocates for the stable genius. For the writing vocation, this means one whose disposition of stability allows him or her to see reality in all its beauty and messiness.
